title: How to Write Better Gemini Notebook Audio Overview Prompts
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Phillip Alcock gives teachers a three-step workflow for shaping a NotebookLM Audio Overview with a prompt that sets an audience, an opening question and a story arc. The idea is adapted from a Reddit suggestion to ask the AI hosts for an introduction, an ending and a podcast-style arc. He explains why each element of the prompt matters: naming the audience controls vocabulary, an opening question gives the discussion focus, and the middle order is a request rather than a guarantee. He adds a careful instruction that disagreements should be discussed only when the sources support them, which reduces invented debates. The workflow supplies a fill-in-the-brackets template, a worked example about plastic waste for primary teachers, and a listen-and-check step against the original sources. Throughout he stresses that restrictions on invented quotations set a boundary but cannot guarantee accuracy, so teachers must verify the audio before sharing it.
points: Naming a specific audience in the prompt controls the vocabulary and depth of the generated discussion, from Year 5 explanations to professional talk for planning teachers.
An opening question must be one the selected sources can actually answer, or the hosts will have too little evidence to draw on.
Telling the hosts to discuss disagreements only where the sources support them reduces the chance of an invented debate.
The reusable template pairs a story arc (background, key ideas, perspectives, recap and closing question) with a source-only restriction.
A restriction against inventing quotations is a boundary, not a guarantee, so the audio must be checked against the sources before it is shared.
quotes: An Audio Overview prompt can guide who the discussion is for, what it focuses on and how the ideas unfold. NotebookLM uses your selected sources as its starting material, while your instructions guide the direction of the audio.
Choose one that your sources can help answer. If the material only describes types of plastic, the hosts may have too little evidence to discuss solutions.
That order is a request, not a guarantee that every generated overview will follow it exactly.
Asking the hosts to discuss disagreements only when the sources support them reduces the chance of encouraging an invented debate.
Telling NotebookLM not to invent quotations or evidence sets a boundary, but it cannot guarantee accuracy. You still need to check claims against the original material.
Tip: Choose sources that contain enough information to answer your opening question. Add another source if an important part of the topic is missing.
Verify any important factual claims and quotations in the original material. If a claim cannot be supported, do not share that version as reliable information.
